items.justification: Orderly network reconnection versus the AI content of a staff security training programme.
Changing an authentication value versus documenting the provenance of public training data.
Guidance aimed at consumers versus threat awareness maintained by an organization's own staff.
Both require users to be told about updates; A covers disruption to functionality, B covers security relevance and explanation.
Both restrict what an attacker can extract through an exposed interface, A by limiting disclosure, B by limiting access rate.
Encryption of security parameters in transit versus an audit log of prompt and configuration changes.
Consumer setup guidance versus logging changes to model configuration.
Publishing the rationale for absent updates versus sanitising data and inputs at design time.
Password generation resistant to automated attack versus general robustness to adversarial AI attacks; B does not name credentials.
Both make automated attack through an exposed interface impracticable, A against brute-forced authentication, B against model access rate.
Both require access control over security-relevant surfaces, A on device configuration interfaces, B on APIs, models and pipelines.
Secure setup guidance versus the risk carried by unused model capabilities.
Both cut attack surface by removing unnecessary capability; A mandates minimizing code, B mandates managing the risk of superfluous model functionality.
Hardware replaceability versus evaluation of access control frameworks.
Lifecycle management of security parameters versus AI content in a training programme.
Documenting sensing capabilities versus publishing hashes of model components.
Vulnerability management of one's own product and due diligence on external components are the two halves of product security assurance across the supply chain.
Disabling unnecessary services versus guidance on appropriate use and failure modes.
Runtime validation of user interface input versus documentation that allows poisoned training data to be traced after the fact.
Checking for available updates versus evaluation of access control frameworks.
Use of reviewed cryptographic implementations versus separated development and tuning environments.
Both require secure disposal of data held in back-end services, A on user request, B on transfer of ownership.
Continuous vulnerability monitoring versus a review of organizational access control frameworks.
Automatic update activation versus secure disposal of assets on transfer of ownership.
Authentication before configuration change versus incident management and recovery planning.
Alerting on unauthorized software change versus evaluation of access control frameworks.
Detection of unauthorized change versus justifying the use of poorly documented components.
Recording justifications for non-applicable provisions versus incident and recovery planning.
Per-device password uniqueness versus documenting where public training data came from.
User-side checking and operator-side continuous monitoring are different obligations that together keep a deployed system in a secure state.
Encryption of sensitive personal data in transit versus the delivery chain for security patches.
Uniqueness of security parameters versus the risk of unused model capability.
Rectifying vulnerabilities and notifying users of the resulting security updates are consecutive steps of one handling process.
Password generation mechanism versus an audit log of model configuration changes.
Recognizable model designation on a device versus logging changes to system prompts.
Both mandate least privilege, A for software running on the device, B for development and tuning environments.
Documenting sensing capabilities versus supporting users through an incident.
Prohibiting hard-coded security parameters versus publishing hashes for model components.
Cryptography for the update mechanism versus general robustness of the AI system to adversarial input.
Orderly network reconnection versus cryptographic hashes for model components.
